4. The trial court dismissed the suit. On appeal, the trial Court's judgment was reversed and the suit was decreed. On the defendant's Second Appeal to the High Court of East Pakistan a Division Bench of the Court set aside the decree of the first appellate court and dismissed the suit as non-maintainable for not impleading Nalini Bala Roy in the suit. 

 5. The plaintiff, thereafter, sought leave to appeal from the judgment of the High Court on the ground that Nalini Bala having transferred her title to the disputed property to the plaintiff and the latter having stepped into her shoes, the former was not a necessary party to the suit and that the learned Judges of the High Court were not right in dismissing the suit as non-maintainable for non-joinder of Nalini Bala. The leave was granted for consideration if Nalini Bala was a necessary party to the suit and if the High Court was right in dismissing the suit as non-maintainable. 

 6. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in dismissing the suit on the ground that Nalini Bala Roy was a necessary party to the suit and that she should have been impleaded therein. He argued that no objection as regards, defect of party was raised by the defendant in the suit. For the first time before the High Court this objection was raised. He pointed out that Order 1 rule 13 C.P.C. provides that objection as to non-joinder of parties must be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and objection not so taken must be deemed to have been waived. In this connection he referred to the issues framed by the trial court. The issues are as follows:- 

 7. With reference to the above issues it was urged that no issue as to defect of party was framed. Therefore, he tried to impress upon us that the defendant raised no objection that Nalini Bala Roy was a necessary party and that she should have been made a party in the suit. It is true that no specific issue as regards non-joinder of Nalini Bala was raised but it appears that an issue to the effect that the suit was barred under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act was framed. This was issue No. 3. It is an admitted fact that Nalini Bala entered into an agreement with the defendant for sale of the suit properly for a consideration of Rs. 3,000/- and in pursuance of the said agreement the defendant was given possession of the property in March, 1951. The defendant paid Rs. 1,000/- in cash on the date of agreement. The defendant further asserted that in addition to payment of Rs. 1,000/- he also paid Rs. 660/- on one occasion, Rs. 700/- on another occasion and lastly Rs. 500/- and in all he paid Rs. 2,860/- towards the consideration of the property. He was ready to perform his part of the contract and served notice upon Nalini Bala Roy asking her to complete her part of the contract. Having been inducted in possession of the suit property in pursuance of the contract for sale of the property he has been maintaining his possession of the property and he claimed that he had a right to be in such possession under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act. It is thus obvious that though specifically no issue was framed as regards defect of party Issue No. 3 sufficiently indicated that the person against whom the defendant was claiming his right and protection under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act ought to have been made a party in the suit. The learned Munsif found that the defendant was and is still willing to perform his part of the contract. The only person to refute this contention of the defendant was Nalini Bala Roy. Necessarily it follows that Nalini Bala Roy should have been impleaded as a party to the suit. The High Court also held that the defendant relied on the very contract between him and Nalini Bala Roy and the defendant contended that he performed his part of the contract and invoked section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act to maintain his possession. In this view of the matter the High Court held that no effective decree could be passed in the absence of Nalini Bala Roy. In this view of the matter it dismissed the suit. 

 8. Mr. Asrarul Hossain next contended that Order 1 rule 9 provides that no suit shall be defeated by reason of non-joinder of parties, and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interest of the parties actually before it. He further contended that this rule should be read along with rule 10(2) which gives wide powers to the court to remedy non-joinder of parties by adding necessary parties, if there be any. The High Court itself referred to rule 10(2) of Order 1 in its judgment. This rule enables in the absence of that person to effectively and completely adjudicate upon and settle the questions involved in the suit. In this view of the matter the learned counsel urged that the High Court should not have dismissed the suit even if it were of the view that Nalini Bala Roy was a necessary party. The High Court could have, instead of dismissing the suit, disposed of the appeal in an appropriate manner. He, however, made an endeavor to impress upon us that Nalini Bala was not a necessary party as she was no longer bound by the contract cancelled by her and sold the property to the plff-appellant for valuable consideration. 

 9. Mr. M.H. Khondkar, learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that in pursuance of the contract entered into between Nalini Bala Roy and the defendant in respect of sale of the suit property, the latter having been inducted in possession of the land in part performance of the contract and still continuing in possession on the basis of the alleged deal of the property is entitled to resist the claim of the plaintiff who is none but a trustee for the defendant under section 3 and illustration 'g' of the Specific Relief Act. The defendant cannot, therefore, be evicted so long the contract between him and Nalini Bala Roy is not legally terminated or cancelled. He submitted that the contract is still subsisting and defendant is protected under section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
